findings.text: In its first paragraph the page says what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. A newcomer can repeat all three after a single read.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: A newcomer who arrives at Athena's home URL finds a page whose title is about a different project, firstmate. The second and third lede paragraphs explain why, but the title alone suggests they are on the wrong page.
findings.source:
Athena explains how firstmate handles work

and "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: A link near the top jumps to concrete next steps: the repository, the clone command, the prerequisites, ./setup.sh and a sample `athena ask "add a changelog"`. The newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The prerequisites come after the clone step, so a reader working down the list finds them late. The list never says what setup.sh installs or where it puts it.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone ..." listed before "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: The page shows Athena's ability to read and explain a project, but nothing of its main promise: a commit traced to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict. A newcomer never sees what that trace looks like.
findings.source: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost" vs. the body, which is a study of firstmate

findings.text: A first-time visitor is not the owner, so this link in the header is puzzling. It reads as an internal admin link.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed firstmate state machine (exit 75, places-held, pending-close records). That depth has little value to a newcomer judging Athena, except as proof that every statement is cited. The "Start here" section and the glossary keep it readable.
Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to file lines at a pinned commit. This shows the traceability promised in the opening paragraphs, and a skeptical newcomer can check it.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it" and claim links such as "AGENTS.md:206-206"

findings.text: The "About this page" section and the footer use repository-internal terms that mean nothing to a newcomer. The page also never says how a reader would ask Athena to make a study like this one.
findings.source: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
